keyIdeas: Water moves into and out of the air around us every day.
Water that dries up has not disappeared forever.

askTeacherContext.summary: This opening introduces the water cycle using two everyday Ghanaian examples: wet clothes drying on a line and water droplets forming on the outside of a cold sachet of water. Water on drying clothes does not vanish; it changes into invisible gas in the air. Droplets outside a cold sachet do not leak from inside; they come from water vapour already in the warm air.

seedFaqs.q: Does water from wet clothes really not disappear?
seedFaqs.a: No, it never disappears. Heat from the sun changes the liquid water into an invisible gas that moves into the air.

seedFaqs.q: Why does my cold sachet water get wet on the outside if it has no hole?
seedFaqs.a: Warm air around the sachet holds invisible water vapour. When that vapour touches the cold plastic, it cools and turns into tiny liquid drops.

seedFaqs.q: Why do clothes dry faster in the sun than in the shade?
seedFaqs.a: The sun gives more heat energy, which helps liquid water turn into gas much faster.

askTeacherContext.outOfScopeRule: That is an interesting question, but right now we are focusing on how water moves in the water cycle. Please ask your classroom teacher later.

keyIdeas: Water exists as solid (ice), liquid (water), and gas (water vapour).
Pure water vapour is an invisible gas.

askTeacherContext.summary: Water exists in three states: solid (ice), liquid (drinking water), and gas (water vapour). Pure water vapour is invisible. Adding heat melts solid ice into liquid water and changes liquid water into water vapour. Cooling changes water vapour back into liquid water and freezes liquid water into ice. White mist above a boiling kenkey pot is tiny cooled liquid droplets, not pure invisible vapour.

seedFaqs.q: If water vapour is invisible, why can I see mist above a boiling kenkey pot?
seedFaqs.a: Great question! The mist you see above the pot is actually tiny liquid droplets that already cooled slightly in the air. Pure water vapour right at the surface is invisible.

seedFaqs.q: Is water vapour still water?
seedFaqs.a: Yes. It is the exact same water, just spread out as a gas instead of flowing as a liquid.

seedFaqs.q: What makes water change from one state to another?
seedFaqs.a: Adding heat energy or taking heat away by cooling makes water change its state.

askTeacherContext.outOfScopeRule: Let us keep our focus on how water changes between solid, liquid, and gas. For other topics, please ask your classroom teacher.

The four main stages are evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection.

askTeacherContext.summary: The water cycle is the continuous, repeated movement of water between the Earth's surface and the sky. Its four main stages in clockwise order are evaporation (water rises as vapour), condensation (vapour cools to form clouds), precipitation (water falls as rain or hail), and collection (water gathers in rivers, lakes, the sea, and underground). Because it is a cycle, it has no true starting or ending point.

seedFaqs.q: Does the water cycle ever stop?
seedFaqs.a: No. As long as the sun shines and there is water on Earth, the water cycle keeps repeating day after day.

seedFaqs.q: Which stage is the very first stage of the water cycle?
seedFaqs.a: Because a cycle is a circle, it has no true start or end. Teachers often begin with evaporation to make it easy to follow.

seedFaqs.q: How can I remember the four stage names?
seedFaqs.a: Think of the direction: rising up is evaporation, forming clouds is condensation, falling rain is precipitation, and gathering on Earth is collection.

narration.ttsText: Let us look closely at evaporation. Evaporation happens when heat from the sun warms liquid water and turns it into invisible water vapour, which rises into the sky. Remember your wet school uniform hanging in the sun? That water did not disappear. It evaporated into the air. Some people think only the sea takes part in the water cycle, but that is not true. keyIdeas: Evaporation is liquid water turning into water vapour due to heat from the sun.
Evaporation happens from seas, lakes, rivers, puddles, wet clothes, and soil — not only the sea.
Transpiration is water vapour released into the air by plant leaves.

askTeacherContext.summary: Evaporation is the process by which heat energy from the sun turns liquid water into invisible water vapour that rises into the air. It occurs from oceans, Lake Volta, rivers, puddles, damp soil, and drying clothes — not just the sea. Plants also release water vapour into the air through tiny openings in their leaves; this process is called transpiration.

seedFaqs.q: Does water have to boil before it can evaporate?
seedFaqs.a: No! Water evaporates slowly at ordinary warm temperatures too, which is why puddles and wet clothes dry without boiling.

seedFaqs.q: What is the difference between evaporation and transpiration?
seedFaqs.a: Evaporation is water turning into vapour from open surfaces like lakes or clothes. Transpiration is water vapour escaping from plant leaves.

seedFaqs.q: Why does windy weather help water evaporate faster?
seedFaqs.a: Wind blows away the damp air above the water, making room for more liquid water to turn into vapour.

askTeacherContext.outOfScopeRule: Right now we are studying evaporation and transpiration in the water cycle. Please ask your teacher if you want to explore another topic.

slides.teacherNote: Explicitly counter the misconception that only the sea evaporates. Point out nearby trees or school garden crops as sources of transpiration.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Say clearly and curiously, pausing before explaining what clouds are made of:
narration.script: What happens after water vapour rises into the sky? Higher up above the Earth, the air is much cooler. When warm water vapour reaches that cool air, it loses heat and changes back into millions of tiny liquid water droplets. Scientists call this change condensation. Look at the magnified circle on the right. Those tiny droplets group together to form clouds. Very high, freezing clouds can also hold tiny ice crystals, but clouds are made mostly of water droplets, never smoke from fires! You see condensation on the ground too, as morning mist on hills or drops outside a cold sachet of water.
narration.ttsText: What happens after water vapour rises into the sky? Higher up above the Earth, the air is much cooler. When warm water vapour reaches that cool air, it loses heat and changes back into millions of tiny liquid water droplets. Scientists call this change condensation. Look at the magnified circle on the right. Those tiny droplets group together to form clouds. Very high, freezing clouds can also hold tiny ice crystals, but clouds are made mostly of water droplets, never smoke from fires! You see condensation on the ground too, as morning mist on hills or drops outside a cold sachet of water.

keyIdeas: Condensation is water vapour cooling down to become tiny liquid droplets.
Clouds are made mostly of tiny water droplets (and tiny ice crystals in very high clouds), not smoke.
Morning mist and drops on a cold sachet are everyday examples of condensation.

askTeacherContext.summary: Condensation happens when warm, invisible water vapour rises into cooler air high in the sky, loses heat, and turns back into millions of tiny liquid water droplets. These droplets group together to form clouds. Very high clouds can also contain tiny ice crystals. Clouds are made of water, not smoke. Condensation also happens near the ground as morning mist on hills or drops on a cold sachet of water.

seedFaqs.q: Why do clouds stay floating in the sky if they are made of liquid water?
seedFaqs.a: Each droplet inside a cloud is so tiny and light that moving air easily holds it up.

seedFaqs.q: Are clouds made of smoke?
seedFaqs.a: No. Smoke comes from burning and contains tiny bits of ash. Clouds are made mostly of tiny water droplets formed by condensation.

seedFaqs.q: Can a cloud ever contain ice?
seedFaqs.a: Yes! Very high up in the sky where the air is freezing cold, clouds can contain tiny ice crystals as well as water droplets.

askTeacherContext.summary: Precipitation occurs when tiny droplets in a cloud collide, combine, and grow too heavy to stay suspended in the air, so gravity pulls them to Earth. seedFaqs.q: Why does it sometimes rain hail in Ghana even though Ghana is warm?
seedFaqs.a: High up inside tall storm clouds, the air is freezing cold. Water droplets can freeze into small ice balls called hail before falling quickly to the ground.

seedFaqs.q: Why is there almost no rain during Harmattan?
seedFaqs.a: Harmattan winds blow from dry desert areas, so the air carries very little water vapour to form rain clouds.

seedFaqs.q: Why does rain stop after a while?
seedFaqs.a: Once most of the heavy water droplets have fallen out of the cloud, the cloud thins out and the rain stops.

Surface run-off flows over the land into streams, rivers, and lakes.

askTeacherContext.summary: Collection is the stage where fallen rainwater gathers on Earth. Part of it flows across the land as surface run-off into streams, rivers, lakes (such as Lake Volta and Lake Bosomtwe), and the ocean. Another part soaks down through tiny spaces in soil and rocks to form groundwater, which fills wells and boreholes. Borehole water is safe to drink when the borehole is properly protected and tested.

seedFaqs.q: How can water fit underground if the ground is solid rock and soil?
seedFaqs.a: Soil and many rocks have millions of tiny spaces and cracks between their grains, like a hard sponge, where groundwater can collect.

seedFaqs.q: Why does rainwater sometimes flood our streets instead of soaking in?
seedFaqs.a: Concrete roads, tarred surfaces, and blocked gutters stop water from soaking into the soil, so more water becomes fast surface run-off.

seedFaqs.q: Is borehole water always safe to drink without checking?
seedFaqs.a: No. Borehole water is safe when the borehole is properly built, kept away from waste, and tested regularly.

askTeacherContext.outOfScopeRule: Let us keep our questions focused on collection, surface run-off, and groundwater. Ask your teacher for other topics.

seedFaqs.q: How do clouds move from the sea or a lake to farms far inland?

seedFaqs.q: If a drop of water evaporates from the salty sea, why is rain not salty?

seedFaqs.q: What would happen to the water cycle if the sun stopped shining?
seedFaqs.a: Without the sun's heat energy, water would stop evaporating and eventually freeze, so the water cycle would stop.

seedFaqs.q: If Earth never loses its water, why do we still worry about water shortages?
seedFaqs.a: Even though total water on Earth stays the same, safe fresh water in one town can run low during dry seasons or become too polluted to drink.

seedFaqs.q: Does gravity also help the water cycle repeat?
seedFaqs.a: Yes! Gravity pulls heavy rain droplets down from clouds and pulls rivers downhill toward lakes and the sea.

seedFaqs.q: Is rainwater from our roof safe to drink right away?
seedFaqs.a: No. Roof rainwater can pick up dust or dirt from the roof, so it should be filtered or boiled before drinking.

seedFaqs.q: What happens to farms if the rainy season starts very late?
seedFaqs.a: Seeds cannot sprout well and young crops dry out, which leads to smaller harvests and higher food prices.

seedFaqs.q: Do plants need the water cycle for anything besides drinking?
seedFaqs.a: Yes! Plants use water to make their own food using sunlight and to carry nutrients up from the soil.

narration.script: The water cycle is just as vital for nature as it is for people. items.question: When liquid water is heated strongly by the sun, what invisible state does it change into?

options.text: Solid ice crystals
Tiny mist droplets
Water vapour
White cooking steam

items.explanation: Heating liquid water turns it into water vapour, which is an invisible gas in the air.

onCorrect.text: Well done! Heat turns liquid water into invisible water vapour.

onWrong.hintText: Ice forms when water cools down, not when it is heated. Look for the invisible gas state.
onWrong.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing heating with cooling state changes

onWrong.hintText: Mist droplets are tiny liquids you can see. Look for the invisible gas form of water.
onWrong.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing visible mist droplets with invisible water vapour

onWrong.hintText: White steam above a pot is cooled liquid droplets you can see. Pure gas water is invisible.
onWrong.misconceptionTargeted: Believing water vapour is visible white steam

items.prompt: Put the four stages of the water cycle in the right clockwise order, starting with water rising from a lake.
items.explanation: Heat lifts water by evaporation, cool air forms clouds by condensation, heavy drops fall as precipitation, and water gathers through collection.

onCorrect.text: Spot on! Evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection repeat in that clockwise order.

onWrong.hintText: Follow one drop: first it rises up, then it forms a cloud, then it falls as rain, and last it gathers on Earth.
onWrong.misconceptionTargeted: Misordering the four stages of the water cycle

items.question: Kwame buys a cold sachet of water on a hot afternoon. Soon, tiny water drops appear on the outside of the sealed plastic. Which stage caused these drops?

options.text: Condensation
Evaporation from inside
Transpiration through plastic
Precipitation from above

items.explanation: Warm water vapour in the air cooled when it touched the cold sachet and turned into liquid drops — that is condensation.

onCorrect.text: Excellent thinking! Cooling vapour into liquid drops is condensation.

onWrong.hintText: The sachet is sealed and evaporation turns liquid into gas. Here, gas in the air cooled into drops.
onWrong.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing evaporation with condensation or assuming the sachet leaks

onWrong.hintText: Transpiration only happens from plant leaves, not plastic bags. Look for cooling vapour into drops.
onWrong.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing transpiration with condensation

onWrong.hintText: Precipitation falls from clouds in the sky. Here, drops formed directly on a cold surface.
onWrong.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing surface condensation with precipitation

items.question: Why does rain fall from clouds to the ground?

options.text: Clouds bump together until they burst open.
Clouds are made of smoke that cools into water.
Wind pushes water down from tall mountains.
Cloud droplets join and grow too heavy.

items.explanation: As tiny water droplets inside a cloud bump and join, they grow too heavy for the air to hold and gravity pulls them down.

onCorrect.text: Right! Rain falls when cloud droplets join and become too heavy to stay up.

onWrong.hintText: Clouds are not solid bags that burst! Think about what happens when tiny droplets join together.
onWrong.misconceptionTargeted: Thinking clouds are containers or tanks that burst open

onWrong.hintText: Clouds are made mostly of water droplets, not smoke. Why do those droplets start falling?
onWrong.misconceptionTargeted: Clouds are smoke

onWrong.hintText: Wind moves clouds across the sky, but gravity pulls heavy droplets downward as rain.
onWrong.misconceptionTargeted: Thinking wind pushes rain down from mountains

items.question: A school in Northern Ghana pumps safe water from a protected borehole during the dry season. Which water source supplies that borehole?

Underground sea water pumped from the coast

onWrong.hintText: Surface run-off flows on top of the ground. Boreholes reach water stored deep underneath.

onWrong.hintText: Boreholes pump stored liquid water from underground, not condensed vapour inside the pipe.
onWrong.misconceptionTargeted: Believing boreholes condense air into water

onWrong.hintText: Sea water is salty and far away. Boreholes tap fresh rainwater stored underground.
onWrong.misconceptionTargeted: Only the sea supplies underground water

items.question: Why is the water cycle described as a repeated pattern in nature?

options.text: Earth creates brand new water every rainy season.
Only sea water moves up into the sky each year.
The sun's heat recycles the same water.
Clouds always drop the same amount of rain daily.

items.question: Ama hangs her wet school uniform in the sun and later it is dry. What actually happened to the water in the cloth?

onWrong.hintText: Water never disappears forever. It only changes state into an invisible gas.

items.question: Which statement BEST describes why the water cycle is important in nature?

options.text: It refills rivers, wetlands, and habitats.
It turns fresh lakes into salty ocean water.
It keeps rivers full even during long droughts.
It only brings rain to towns near the coast.

items.question: A town cuts down trees along its main river and people dump waste into the stream. What are two likely results?

Dirty river water and muddy run-off.
More rainwater soaking into hard bare soil.
Cleaner drinking water for towns downstream.

onWrong.hintText: Fewer trees mean less transpiration, and dumping waste harms fish habitats.

summary.recapScript: Today you learned that the water cycle is nature's repeated journey of water powered by heat energy from the sun. Through evaporation and transpiration, liquid water rises as invisible vapour. High in cool air, condensation turns vapour into clouds made mostly of tiny droplets. Heavy droplets fall as precipitation, and collection stores water in rivers, lakes, the sea, and underground boreholes. Because this cycle keeps habitats, farms, and hydroelectric dams alive, every one of us must help protect our rivers and trees.
takeaways: The four stages — evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection — repeat continuously using the sun's heat energy.
Earth does not make new water; it recycles the same water across seas, lakes, rivers, soil, clouds, and plants over a very long time.
The water cycle supports natural habitats, weather, drinking water, farming, and hydroelectric power, so we must protect rivers and trees.

extensionActivity.title: Water Cycle in a Bag
materials: One clear, sealable plastic bag (such as a clean zip-lock or knotted transparent polythene bag)
Two tablespoons of clean cool tap water
A sunny window or warm outdoor wall
steps: Pour two tablespoons of clean cool water into the clear plastic bag.
Seal the bag tightly so no air or water vapour can escape.
Use sticky tape to fasten the top of the bag flat against a sunny window.
Check the bag after one hour, three hours, and at the end of the afternoon, and draw what you see in your science notebook.
extensionActivity.safetyNote: Use only clean, cool water — never hot water. Keep plastic bags away from babies and small children, and dispose of or reuse the bag responsibly after the experiment.
extensionActivity.expectedObservation: Warm sunlight causes some water at the bottom to evaporate into invisible vapour. Near the cooler upper plastic, tiny misty droplets form by condensation. When droplets join and grow heavy, they trickle down the inside of the bag like precipitation back into the pool (collection).
